name: Contractor safety prequalification
summary: For a named job, the operations, facilities or site manager gets a safety questionnaire scaled to the risk of the work, then a record of the contractor's answers scored only on the evidence supplied, with every gap, the conditions that close it and a review date. A competent person decides.

sources.title: Fully Powered AI's own rules for this work: Met, Partly met and Gap with what each means; must-pass questions and stop findings kept as company settings, with a mechanical outcome rule and a blank decision line for the competent person; insurance set against the company's minimums, like with like; trade competence scored apart from the certification for each dangerous activity; the people list with stated column headers; claims not counted, quoted; checks only a person can make, listed apart; points the rules cannot settle; owners and dates taken only from the brief and settings; the review date counted from the job's last day; and no law or standard cited.

sources.contribution: A questionnaire to send and a scored record of the answers; three tiers of questions set by the most dangerous task in the job; scoring only what the documents show, so an unsupported answer is a gap; dangerous work never passed on protective equipment or experience alone; approve, conditional or reject, decided by a competent person; people in incident records reduced to labels.

Naming the contractor, the job and the site before anything is scored; insurance, the safety record and trade competence as the documents needed before any outcome; who else could be affected; new approval or renewal; the decision maker and the review period; examples of low- and medium-risk work for the tiers.

A check before anything is returned: every score tied to evidence, no approval over an open gap, dangerous work not passed on protective equipment or competence claims, the tier set by the riskiest activity, a review date set, people hurt in incidents not named, and the real contractor, job and site named rather than a generic questionnaire.
Personal details found and named before anything else is written, people replaced by stable labels, and the originals kept apart from the record.

A core question set for every contractor, more for skilled trades and an added set for dangerous activities, each with the document that answers it; the claim, the evidence and its status kept for each item; rejection when a point fails beyond repair, such as no insurance; a review timed by whichever document expires first, or by a fixed period; on renewal, expired documents counted as gaps again.
A stated scoring rule and a named decision maker, so two reviewers reach the same result; subcontracting and supervision of the crew as questions that are easy to leave out.
The hard cases of a certificate claimed but not supplied, one contractor on a low-risk and a high-risk job, and an injured worker named in the records, used here as acceptance tests in new scenarios.

A worked case in which work at height and an unproven certificate lead to a conditional outcome; work held until the conditions close; certificates checked with the body that issued them; a review at the first expiry or after twelve months, whichever comes first.

A questionnaire that opens with directions to the contractor and closes with a signed declaration, with questions on rescue plans, permits, inspection of access equipment and controls put in place ahead of protective equipment.

A return date for the contractor's answers and a fresh look at the questions when the scope of the job changes, both named as things a questionnaire should carry; first aid on site among the questions a company may add.
The order of the record: the job and its tier, the questions with the evidence each needs, the register of what was supplied, the gaps, the outcome with its conditions, and sign-off.
